NoteSummary

I analysed a year of purchasing records from a multinational coatings and paints manufacturer: 251,734 order lines and 1.6 million recorded steps. The goal was to find where the order-to-payment process slows down, where work is redone, and whether the company’s payment controls are followed.

  • Order lines that are corrected after ordering take 19 days (25%) longer to pay. About 1 in 10 lines is corrected.
  • Recording an invoice before the goods arrive does not slow payment down, but it puts the payment on hold 97% of the time, and a person has to release that hold in 43.5% of these lines, compared with 17.2% otherwise.
  • The strictest payment control is followed 100% of the time and costs no extra time.
  • Ten process paths cover 60% of all order lines, out of 11,912 distinct paths.

My hypothesis was partly supported: price and quantity changes do slow payment; invoicing before goods receipt does not.

1 The business problem

Every company that buys materials follows the same routine, called purchase-to-pay:

  1. Order. Someone creates a purchase order with a supplier.
  2. Receive. The supplier delivers, and the warehouse records the goods receipt.
  3. Bill. The supplier sends an invoice, and accounts payable records it.
  4. Pay. The company pays the invoice.

Before paying, most companies run a check called matching: does the invoice agree with what was ordered and what was actually received? This prevents paying for goods that never arrived or paying the wrong price. The company in this dataset uses four kinds of check:

When this process runs badly, cash planning gets harder, accounts payable spends time on manual fixes, and suppliers are paid late or incorrectly. Managers usually see the process as it was designed. System event logs show how it actually runs.

Questions I set out to answer:

  • How long does it take from creating an order to paying for it, and does that differ by matching type?
  • How often is work redone, such as price or quantity corrections?
  • Are the matching controls followed?
  • What does the normal path look like, and which exceptions are common?

Hypothesis. Items with price or quantity changes after the purchase order is created, and items invoiced before goods receipt, take noticeably longer to clear and account for most of the rework.

2 Data and validation

Source. BPI Challenge 2019 event log: purchase order handling at a multinational coatings and paints company, 2018. van Dongen, B.F. (2019). BPI Challenge 2019. 4TU.ResearchData. https://doi.org/10.4121/uuid:d06aff4b-79f0-45e6-8ec8-e19730c248f1

Each case is one purchase order line. Each event is one step in that line’s history (for example “Record Goods Receipt”) with a timestamp. Each case also carries its matching type.

Validation. I loaded the file from a community mirror, so I checked it against the official figures first. The counts match exactly:

Every case has exactly one “Create Purchase Order Item” event, which confirms that one case equals one order line.

Date quality. The data is described as 2018, but timestamps range from 1948 to 2020.

  • 45,137 events fall after 2018, almost all in January 2019. These are 2018 orders that finished after New Year. I kept them, because dropping them would remove the slowest orders and make the process look faster than it is.
  • 318 events fall before 2018, including dates in 1948, 1993 and 2001. These are data-entry errors. I excluded the 264 cases that contain them (0.1% of cases).

After filtering, 251,470 order lines remain. The matching types are very unequal in size:

3 Approach

The analysis is three Python scripts, run in order:

  1. Load and profile (01_load_profile.py). Read the 730 MB event log once, check the counts and dates, and save a 13 MB copy for fast reloading.
  2. Compare matching types (02_matching_types.py). Build one row of measures per order line, compare the four types, and test the hypothesis.
  3. Variants and process map (03_variants.py). Find the distinct paths order lines take, and map the most common ones.

Measures

  • Order-to-payment time: days from the first “Create Purchase Order Item” to the last “Clear Invoice”. Only lines that have both events are measured (183,419 lines).
  • Rework: a price or quantity change, or an unusual repeated step. Steps that legitimately repeat (partial deliveries, instalment invoices, approval rounds) are not counted as rework.
  • Invoice before goods: the first recorded invoice is earlier than the first goods receipt.

Tools: Python, pandas (data tables), pm4py (process mining), matplotlib (charts), Graphviz (process map drawing).

4 Hypothesis result

Partly supported. Price and quantity changes go with clearly slower payment. Invoicing before goods receipt does not.

Invoice-first lines are not slower, but their spread is wider: a quarter of them clear in under 37 days, compared with 56 days for goods-first lines.

5 Findings

5.1 Corrections after ordering are common and slow payment down

  • 10.5% of order lines had their price or quantity changed after the order was created.
  • 2,472 lines had their quantity changed more than once, and 860 their price.
  • 3.5% of lines were deleted after being created. “Order created, then deleted” is the 9th most common path (5,298 lines).
  • Changed lines take a median 19 days longer to pay (Table 4).

5.2 Invoicing before the goods arrive creates payment holds and extra handling, not delay

A payment block holds an invoice until it can be paid. The block can be removed by a person or by an automated batch job. Of the 57,071 block removals in the data, 72.9% were done by people and 27.1% by batch jobs.

  • Invoice-first lines almost always go on hold, and a person releases the hold in 43.5% of them, about 2.5 times the rate for goods-first lines.
  • Overall, 22.2% of order lines had a payment block removed, and 16.1% needed a person to remove it.
  • Lines with a payment block removal took a median 87.0 days to pay, against 72.9 days without. Most of those lines are goods-first, and invoice-first lines themselves are not slower, so the cost of invoicing first is handling effort rather than extra days.

5.3 The strictest control is followed and costs no extra time

  • For “invoice after goods receipt” lines, the invoice was never recorded before the goods (0.0% of 11,078 lines). The system enforces the rule.
  • Where the lenient type allows invoicing first, it happened in only 8.2% of lines.
  • Median order-to-payment time is almost identical for the two 3-way types: 77.3 days (lenient) and 79.5 days (strict).

5.4 A few standard paths carry most of the volume

  • The 251,470 order lines follow 11,912 distinct paths.
  • 7 paths cover half of all lines, and the top 10 cover 59.5%.
  • 75.3% of paths (8,974) occur only once. These one-off exceptions add up to just 3.6% of lines.
  • The most common path (20.0% of lines) is: order → supplier invoices → goods received → invoice recorded → paid.

Reading the map:

  • Suppliers often invoice before delivering. That is normal supplier behaviour; the company still records the invoice after the goods arrive in most cases.
  • “Remove Payment Block” sits between invoice recording and payment for about 28,000 of these lines, which makes it a visible extra step. About three-quarters of all block removals are done by people; the rest by automated batch jobs.
  • 12,214 lines stop after the goods receipt. Most are consignment items, which are invoiced elsewhere; the rest were still open when the data was extracted.

6 Recommendations

A supporting KPI for all three is median order-to-payment days, tracked monthly by matching type (2018 baseline: 77.6 days).

7 Decisions and exclusions

8 Limitations

  • Why things happen. The log shows that a price changed or a payment was blocked, not the reason. The findings are comparisons, not proof of cause.
  • Supplier lead time vs internal delay. Order-to-payment time includes delivery time and payment terms, which this data can’t separate from internal slowness.
  • No due dates. I can’t say whether invoices were paid late, early or on time.
  • Open lines at the cut-off. Lines still unpaid when the data ends are left out of time measures, so true times may be somewhat longer.
  • Small groups. 2-way match has only 1,029 lines, and just 289 with a measurable time, so its 7-day median is less reliable.
  • Consignment. There is no invoice clearing at line level, so it has no time or invoice-timing measures.
  • No cost data. The effort of manual fixes can’t be expressed in dollars.
  • Anonymised, one company, one year. Findings can’t be tied to named suppliers or teams and may not generalise.

9 What I would do next

  • Break price and quantity changes down by supplier and spend area to find where corrections concentrate.
  • Measure how long a payment block holds a line, from block to release.
  • Draw a separate process map for each matching type.
  • Weight results by order value, using the net worth field, to show where the money is.

10 How to reproduce

The raw data is not stored in the repository; see data/DOWNLOAD_HERE.md.

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
brew install graphviz
python 01_load_profile.py
python 02_matching_types.py
python 03_variants.py
quarto render case_study.qmd

Step 1 takes about 6 minutes; the others take under 2 minutes.
